```{r}
#| label: setup

library(tidyverse)

who_latest  <- read_rds(here::here("data", "who_latest.rds"))
hackney_col <- "#C8553D"
who_trend   <- read_rds(here::here("data", "who_trend.rds"))
who_trend_gaps <- read_rds(here::here("data", "who_trend_gaps.rds"))
dementia_dx <- read_rds(here::here("data", "dementia_dx_london.rds"))
```

# Who is at risk {scrolling="true"}

## Row

### Column {.tabset width="60%"}

::: {.card title="Latest"}

```{r}
#| label: who-latest
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 6
ggplot(who_latest, aes(x = value, y = fct_rev(area), colour = area)) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = lower_ci, xmax = upper_ci), na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ short_label, scales = "free_x", ncol = 3,
             labeller = label_wrap_gen(width = 24)) +  expand_limits(x = 0) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    n.breaks = 3,
    labels = scales::label_number(suffix = "%", drop0trailing = TRUE),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.12))
  ) +  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(Hackney = hackney_col, London = "grey60", England = "grey60"),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.spacing    = unit(1.2, "lines"),
    plot.margin = margin(5, 15, 5, 5)
  )
```

Panels named after a condition show the share of GP-registered patients with that diagnosis. These rates are crude (not age-standardised), so Hackney's young population lowers them.

Social contact is from 2019/20, the latest year with a Hackney value.

:::

::: {.card title="Over time"}
```{r}
#| label: who-trend
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 6
who_trend |>
  # Reverse so England and London are drawn first and Hackney sits on top
  mutate(area = fct_rev(area)) |>
  arrange(area) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = value, colour = area,
             group = interaction(series, area))) +
  geom_segment(
    data = who_trend_gaps,
    aes(x = year, xend = next_year, y = value, yend = next_value,
        linetype = "Year with no value"),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_point(size = 1.2, na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~ short_label, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3,
             labeller = label_wrap_gen(width = 24)) +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = scales::breaks_width(5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    n.breaks = 3,
    labels = scales::label_number(suffix = "%", drop0trailing = TRUE),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.12))
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(Hackney = hackney_col, London = "grey45", England = "grey75"),
    breaks = c("Hackney", "London", "England")   # legend order
  ) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Year with no value" = "dashed"), name = NULL) +
  guides(linetype = guide_legend(position = "inside")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    legend.position        = "top",
    legend.position.inside = c(0.75, 0.13),
    panel.grid.minor       = element_blank(),
    panel.spacing          = unit(1.2, "lines")
  )
```

Recorded depression rises partly because the register counts adults diagnosed since April 2006, so the window keeps lengthening. NHS Digital warns that 2020/21 GP figures may be inaccurate.

Age has no trend because it comes from a single census. Dashed lines join the years either side of a missing value. Social contact has none for 2020/21, when the survey was voluntary because of COVID; depression has none for 2023/24 in the source data.
:::

### Column {width="40%"}

::: {.card title="Is Hackney’s dementia diagnosis rate unusual for London?"}

```{r}
#| label: dementia-dx
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 6
dx_band    <- filter(dementia_dx$band, level == "95")
dx_hackney <- filter(dementia_dx$points, is_hackney)
dx_extremes <- filter(dementia_dx$points, value %in% range(value))

ggplot(dementia_dx$points,
       aes(x = value, y = fct_reorder(area_name, value))) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = dx_band$lower, xmax = dx_band$upper,
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey92") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = dementia_dx$london_avg, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = is_hackney), size = 2.5) +
  geom_text(data = dx_hackney, aes(label = area_name),
            colour = hackney_col, hjust = 1, nudge_x = -3.5, size = 4) +
  geom_text(data = dx_extremes, aes(label = area_name),
            colour = "grey30", hjust = 1, nudge_x = -2, size = 3.5) +
  expand_limits(x = 0) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_number(suffix = "%"),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.05))
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = hackney_col, `FALSE` = "grey60"),
                      guide = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    axis.text.y        = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank()
  )
```

Each dot is a London borough; the line is the London average and the shaded band is the range boroughs typically fall within, not a confidence interval. The rate is diagnosed patients aged 65+ as a share of the estimated number living with dementia, so higher is better. The lowest, the City of London, has an estimated 89 people with dementia, so its rate is far less certain than other boroughs’.


:::

## Row {height="20%"}

::: {.card title="Reading this page"}
The lines through the dots on the Latest tab are 95% intervals, the range of underlying rates consistent with each figure; most are hidden behind the dots because chance makes little difference in populations this large. The shaded band on the diagnosis rate chart is the range London boroughs typically fall within, so a borough outside it differs more than boroughs usually do.
:::

### Column {width="60%"}

::: {.card title="Which neighbourhoods get hottest?"}
Interactive LSOA map goes here, with surface temperature and tree cover as layers you switch between.

Satellites measure how hot surfaces get, not the air people feel. Tree cover data are from 2013.

Line chart of days above 25°C per year since 1960 goes here, averaged over the HadUK-Grid cells covering Hackney.
:::

# Data and methods

## Row {.tabset height="85%"}

::: {.card title="Sources"}

| Source | What it gives | Period | Geography | Licence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| OHID Fingertips | GP-recorded prevalence, dementia diagnosis rate, social contact | Varies by indicator | Borough | Open Government Licence |
| Census 2021 (Nomis) | Age, older people living alone | 2021 | LSOA | Open Government Licence |

Remaining rows from the plan's data sources table go here.
:::

::: {.card title="Methods"}
**Confidence intervals.** What the 95% interval means, in two or three sentences.

**Funnel plots and overdispersion.** How the limits are drawn, why they're widened, and why only two indicators get a funnel.

**Crude rates.** Why GP prevalence isn't age-standardised, and what that means in a young borough.

**Surface temperature.** Which Landsat summer was used, how it's averaged to LSOAs, and that it measures surfaces rather than air.

**Bivariate bands.** How the three bands are drawn across Hackney's LSOAs.

**Change of data source.** Fingertips is being replaced by Find public health data; which one this dashboard uses.
:::

::: {.card title="Limitations"}
**Who is at risk**

- **Crude rates.** One sentence.
- **GP registers count diagnoses.** One sentence.
- **Evidence comes from elsewhere.** One sentence.

**Where it's hot and where they overlap**

- **Surface, not air, temperature.** One sentence.
- **Old tree cover data.** One sentence.
- **Bands are relative to Hackney.** One sentence.
- **Care homes in Census counts.** One sentence.
- **Ecological fallacy.** One sentence.

**What's missing**

- **No indoor overheating data.** One sentence.
- **No local heat death figures.** One sentence.
:::
